pedagogy.summary: Children calculate how long an event lasts from its start and end times. The reliable method is counting ON from the start to the end on a number line — jumping to the next o'clock (a number bond to 60), then whole hours, then the remaining minutes — NOT column subtraction, which fails when the hour is crossed because time is base-60, not base-10. Comparing two durations then follows from calculating each.
bestPractices: Count on from start to end via a number line: bridge to the next o'clock, add whole hours, add the remaining minutes
Make explicit WHY column subtraction fails when hours are crossed (60, not 100)
Use number bonds to 60 for the 'to the next hour' jump
Anchor in real start/end times (lessons, TV programmes)
Calculate both durations before comparing which is longer
keyRepresentations: Blank number line with jumps (to next o'clock, whole hours, remaining minutes)
Analogue / digital clocks showing start and end
Number bond to 60 for the bridging jump
commonMisconceptions: Uses column subtraction of end minus start, which breaks across the hour boundary
Thinks a later end time automatically means a longer duration
Works in 100s not 60s (treats the minutes as base-10)
Counts in the wrong direction or forgets the bridging jump to the o'clock

learn.summary: Children calculate how long an event lasts from its start and end times by counting ON from start to end on a number line: first bridge to the next o'clock (a number bond to 60), then add whole hours, then add the remaining minutes. Make explicit WHY column subtraction breaks when the end minutes are smaller than the start minutes, so you have to borrow across the hour (e.g. 4:10 − 2:50). Time is base-60 (60 minutes in an hour), not base-10. Comparing two durations follows from calculating each; a later end time does not by itself mean a longer duration.

activities.title: Build the jumps on a number line
feedback: General bridging slip (applies to any start time): if the learner makes the jump to the next o'clock too large — e.g. treating 10:15 → 11:00 as +85, or jumping 2:50 → 3:00 by more than +10 — remind them the minutes only run to 60. For 2:50 the jump to 3:00 is +10 (50 + 10 = 60); for 10:15 the jump to 11:00 is +45 (15 + 45 = 60).

If they skip the o'clock jump and land on the wrong minute, rebuild the three-part jump for the activity's own example: next o'clock first (2:50 → 3:00), then whole hours (3:00 → 4:00), then leftover minutes (4:00 → 4:10).

Column slip (a misconception, not a valid method): if, on the activity's 4:10 − 2:50 line-up or any hour-crossing subtraction, they 'borrow' as in base-10 (producing results like 0:85 for 11:00 − 10:15), show that base-10 borrowing assumes 100 minutes in an hour. An hour is 60 minutes, so counting on across the o'clock is the safe method.
activities.rationale: Seeing the jumps assemble the total, and seeing how column subtraction misleads at the minutes column, makes the base-60 structure visible as the child acts. Where a build-your-own number line is available, dragging each jump from the start time with an auto-shown bond to 60 and a running total, plus a 'try column subtraction' option that lines up end minus start, may make the mechanism concrete; a static annotated number line can show one worked example but cannot let the child build the jumps.
sourceClaims: White Rose Y3 Time (Steps 8-9) documents that children may think an event ending at a later time must have a longer duration, and may attempt to calculate duration using column subtraction (end minus start), which leads to problems when hours are crossed; the recommended model is a number line with jumps and number bonds to the next hour.

Children apply discrete whole-number, base-10 reasoning to time and cannot easily coordinate its base-60 groupings, which explains column-subtraction errors and base-10 slips when crossing the hour boundary.
learnerActions: Start at the first time (e.g. 2:50) on a blank number line.
Make the first jump to the next o'clock (2:50 → 3:00, a +10 jump) and say the number bond to 60 that produced it (50 + 10 = 60).
Keep a running total of the jumps to assemble the duration (1 hour 20 minutes).

Compare this count-on method with column subtraction: line up 4:10 − 2:50 and notice the minutes column needs borrowing, and that borrowing as if there were 100 minutes in an hour goes wrong, because the minutes are base-60, not base-10.
activities.intendedInsight: Counting on from start to end — bridging the o'clock, adding whole hours, then the remaining minutes — gives the duration reliably, and column subtraction misleads across the hour unless you remember an hour holds 60 minutes, not 100.

activities.title: Calculate then compare two durations
feedback: If the learner picks the activity that ends later without calculating, have them count on for BOTH events first, then compare the two lengths.
Use a short activity that ends late against a long one that ends early (e.g. the 8:55–9:00 versus 8:00–8:50 pair) to decouple end-time from duration.
On the crossing-the-hour item (2:50 → 4:10), a base-10 or nonsense answer signals column subtraction — return to counting on and the o'clock bridge.
activities.rationale: Anchoring problems in real start/end times (lessons, films, TV programmes) and requiring both durations to be calculated before comparing targets the 'later end = longer' misconception directly. Crossing-the-hour and decoupled end-time items are natural discriminators. These can be posed as questions, fill-in-the-blank sums, or spoken word problems; a character can pose start/end problems but cannot observe the counting-on method, so pair posed problems with the learner showing their jumps.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils should 'compare durations of events [for example, to calculate the time taken by particular events or tasks]'.

White Rose Y3 Time (Steps 8-9) documents that children may think an event ending at a later time must have a longer duration, and may attempt to calculate duration using column subtraction (end minus start), which leads to problems when hours are crossed; the recommended model is a number line with jumps and number bonds to the next hour.
learnerActions: Read a problem such as 'A lesson starts at 10:15 and ends at 11:00 — how long is it?' and count on to find 45 minutes.
Work a crossing-the-hour problem: 'A film starts at 2:50 and ends at 4:10 — how long is it?' bridging to 3:00, adding 1 hour, then +10 to reach 1 hour 20 minutes.
Compare two events, e.g. an activity from 2:20 to 3:00 versus one from 6:15 to 6:50, by calculating each duration (40 minutes vs 35 minutes) and only then deciding which is longer.
Test a tricky comparison: a 5-minute activity ending at 9:00 (so 8:55–9:00) versus one running 8:00 to 8:50 (50 minutes) — which is longer, and which ends later?
activities.intendedInsight: To compare durations you must calculate each one and compare the lengths; the event that ends later is not automatically the longer one.

constraints: Use number bonds to 60 (not 100) for the jump to the next o'clock; the minutes column does not carry in base-10.

Analogue/digital clocks showing start and end, and a blank number line with labelled jumps, support the method; a static worked number line can only annotate one example and cannot let the child build the jumps.

Recognition or multiple-choice items can assess duration and comparison but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction of the three-part jump — have the learner show or build the jumps at least once.
Scaffold the bond-to-60 jump and rehearse the three-part method rather than reteaching clock reading from scratch when the slip is in bridging, not in reading the clock.
Comparing durations depends on first calculating each duration; do not judge 'longer' by the later end time.
Keep every feedback example consistent with its activity's stated setup, or state explicitly that a slip is general to any start/end time.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched and the activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Independent re-audit confirmed all worked examples are internally consistent and all feedback is anchored to its activity's figures or explicitly flagged as a general slip.

The legacy row claimed '3D adds nothing' for this task; that comparative media judgement is not established by the cited sources and has been dropped — duration work is not spatial, but no universal necessity/efficacy claim about any medium is asserted here.

Worked examples checked: 10:15→11:00 = 45 min (15+45=60); 2:50→4:10 = 10 min to 3:00, +1 hour to 4:00, +10 to 4:10 = 1 hour 20 min; 2:20→3:00 = 40 min and 6:15→6:50 = 35 min; 8:55→9:00 = 5 min versus 8:00→8:50 = 50 min. All consistent as stated.

The 0:85-style column result (from 11:00 − 10:15) is retained only as a learner misconception to be corrected, never as a valid method or answer option. Note that for 4:10 − 2:50 correct base-60 borrowing can reach 1:20, so feedback stresses the base-10 vs base-60 borrowing distinction rather than claiming column subtraction always yields a nonsense answer.

probeDeeper: 'Show me the jumps you made — where did you land first?' (o'clock bridge)
'Why doesn't 11:00 take away 10:15 give the answer if you do it in columns?' (base-60)
'This activity ends later — but is it really longer? How long is each one?'
'A 5-minute activity ends at 9:00; another runs 8:00 to 8:50 — which is longer? Which ends later?' (decouples end-time from duration)
assess.correctAnswer: Counts on 10:15 to 11:00 = 45 minutes; for 2:50 to 4:10 bridges to 3:00 (+10), +1 hour to 4:00, +10 = 1 hour 20 minutes; compares the two by their calculated lengths (40 minutes vs 35 minutes), not by which ended later.

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses column subtraction (end minus start), which breaks when hours are crossed
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model counting on via a number line, bridging to the next o'clock; show explicitly that the minutes are base-60, so borrowing 10 doesn't work.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes 4:10 minus 2:50 in columns and borrows base-10, or 11:00 minus 10:15 = 0:85

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks a later end time automatically means a longer duration
errorPatterns.nextMove: Calculate BOTH durations first (count on for each), then compare the lengths; show a short activity that ends late versus a long one that ends early.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the comparison item picks the activity that ends later without calculating each duration

errorPatterns.pattern: Works in 100s not 60s, or forgets the bridging jump — miscounts the step to the next o'clock
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the bond to 60 for the jump to the next o'clock (15 + 45 = 60); rehearse the three-part jump, don't reteach clock reading from scratch.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Bridges 10:15 to the next hour as +85 (base-10), or skips the o'clock jump and lands wrong

responseLevels.gap: Attempts column subtraction; judges 'longer' by the later end; can't cross the hour.
responseLevels.full: Calculates durations by counting on (bridging the o'clock, base-60), crosses the hour reliably, and compares two events by their calculated durations, not their end times.
responseLevels.partial: Counts on correctly within an hour, but slips when the hour is crossed or reverts to column subtraction, or compares by end time.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set duration problems and WATCH the method: (1) 'A lesson starts at 10:15 and ends at 11:00 — how long is it? Show me how you work it out.' (2) A problem that crosses the hour: 'A film starts at 2:50 and ends at 4:10 — how long is it?' (3) 'Which lasted longer — an activity from 2:20 to 3:00, or one from 6:15 to 6:50?' Watch whether they count on (bridging the o'clock) or attempt column subtraction, and whether the comparison rests on calculated durations or on the later end time.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The hour-crossing item (2:50 to 4:10) is the discriminator: a child using column subtraction produces a nonsense or base-10 answer, a child counting on bridges the o'clock correctly. The comparison item catches 'later end = longer'.
